## Project Setup in QGIS

This page will guide you to analyze archaeological features in Echo Mesa using the [orthomosaic](Drone_photogrammetry.qmd) you have just generated. Start QGIS and open a new project. Save it (![](images/clipboard-2987863238.png){width="5%"}) in your Digital Archaeology Lab folder with a filename such as `lab2_EchoMesa_Hopi_Your_LastName.qgz`.

Change the `CRS` to `EPSG:32612` to match that of the orthomosaic.

![Selecting UTM zone 12N for the project](images/clipboard-4056692537.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

As before, from the `Browser` panel, drag a basemap such as `Bing maps` from `XYZ Tiles` to your `Layers`.

![Satellite XYZ tiles in QGIS](images/clipboard-232834069.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

If any of the panels are not there, select `View` -\> `Panels` to toggle them on.

![Panel options](images/clipboard-3835793501.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

## Adding Data

### Orthomosaic and DEM

In QGIS, add both the DEM and orthomosaic `.tif` files as raster layer. In the `Layers` panel, toggle off DEM and compare the resolution between the orthomosaic and the basemap.

::: callout-important
## EXERCISE 2

Compare our 2-cm-resolution drone image to the basemap. List, with screenshots or coordinates, at least three additional features that are only resolved in the orthomosaic.
:::

### Archaeological Features

Next, add `EchoMesa_GroundSurvey.gpkg` that you downloaded as a vector layer. When asked, select all items to add.

![Adding .gpkg to QGIS](images/clipboard-2396376456.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

Next, convert these vectors to UTM zone 12N:

![Converting coordinates between CRSs](images/clipboard-1716612345.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

In the `Layers` panel, select all four vector layers added, right-click on them, and choose `Group Selected`. Name the group as `ground_survey_data`. Now you can toggle on/off all archaeological features at once.

![Grouping layers](images/clipboard-2934135545.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

::: callout-important
## EXERCISE 3

Based on the mapped archaeological features and @herrmann2018, discuss how ultra-high resolution orthoimagery and DEMs we produce using drones can help archaeologists discover, document, and interpret ancient sites and landscapes.
:::

### Thermal Imagery

Finally, add `echocanyon_thermal_8may25_utm.tif` as a raster layer. You may notice that the image looks rather "muted."

![Thermal image initially added to QGIS](images/clipboard-4033755233.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

To troubleshoot, we may need to examine the distribution of the pixel values. Right click on the thermal layer and select `Properties`. In `Layer Properties` window, go to `Histogram` and click `Computer Histogram`.

::: callout-note
For a single-band image such as this thermal image, a GIS program typically maps the range of pixel values onto a grayscale (0-255), from black for the lowest value to white for the highest.
:::

As you can see here, the raster displays poorly because a few outlying values stretch this range. Most pixels fall within only about 10% of it, so they are squeezed into a narrow band of grays, and the variation within the histogram's main peak is hard to see.

![Thermal raster histogram](images/clipboard-1702361124.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

![Thermal raster ideal histogram](images/clipboard-2387496510.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

To change this, go to `Symbology` dialog in `Layer Properties`. In the `Min/Max Value Settings`, select `Cumulative count cut` and choose `10` - `90`%.

![Changing layer symbology in QGIS](images/clipboard-1117125022.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

You should now have a much better visualization of the thermal data.

![Thermal data overlaid by mapped features](images/clipboard-2345076739.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## Archaeology of Echo Mesa

A typical archaeological site in Echo Canyon consists of stone building foundations and artifact scatter at the surface:

![A typical archaeological site in the study region](images/clipboard-2795006388.png){#stone-foundation fig-align="center" width="100%"}

In QGIS map view, one similar site can be found near coordinates `570324.3092,3972901.0257`. Locate this point and set the scale to `1:30`.

![Locating an archaeological site in Echo Mesa](images/clipboard-3256632031.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

Toggle off all layers except for the orthomosaic. Can you see the archaeological feature here?

![An archaeological site in Echo Mesa](images/clipboard-3652846502.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

To map this feature, we will need to create a new vector layer. Go to `Layer` -\> `Create Layer` -\> `New GeoPackage Layer...`. In the pop-up window, first click `...` next to the `File name` and select a location to save your layer with a reasonable name.

For `Geometry type`, select `Polygon`, and select `Project CRS`. In `New Field`, write `ID` in the `Name` field and change `Type` to `Integer`. Press `Add to Fields List`. Finally, press `OK`.

![](images/clipboard-834352606.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

In the `Layers` panel, right-click on the newly created layer and select `Toggle Editing` (![](images/clipboard-472253616.png){width="5%"}). This will let you edit the `.gpkg` file directly. In the top toolbars, select `Add Polygon Feature` (![](images/clipboard-3529096093.png){width="5%"}) and start tracing the boundary of the archaeological site. Once done, hold `Ctrl` and click anywhere on the map. In the pop-up window, put `0` in the `ID` field, indicating this is the first site you map.

![Adding new features to QGIS](images/clipboard-3274568731.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

There you go — you have just mapped your first archaeological feature in QGIS! It should look something like this:

![Your first mapped archaeological site!](images/clipboard-2727169148.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

Once you are done, select `Save Layer Edits` (![](images/clipboard-781940283.png){width="5%"}) in the top toolbar. Click `Toggle Editing` (![](images/clipboard-472253616.png){width="5%"}) again to exit edit mode.

::: callout-important
